About the IACC  
The Interagency Autism Coordinating Committee (IACC) is a federal advisory committee charged with 
coordinating federal activities concerning autism spectrum disorder (ASD) and providing advice to the 
Secretary of Health and Human Services (HHS) on issues related to autism. The Committee was established by 
Congress under the Children’s Health Act of 2000 (Public Law 106-310), reconstituted under the Combating 
Autism Act (CAA) of 2006 (Public Law 109-416), and renewed most recently under the Autism Collaboration, 
Accountability, Research, Education, and Support (CARES) Act of 2024 (Public Law 118-180). This report was 
prepared by the IACC serving under the Autism CARES Act of 2019. 
Membership of the Committee includes a wide array of federal agencies involved in autism research and 
services, as well as public stakeholders, including autistic adults, family members of those on the autism 
spectrum, advocates, service providers, and researchers. The IACC membership is composed to ensure that 
the Committee is equipped to address the broad range of issues and challenges faced by individuals and 
families in the autism community.  
Under the Autism CARES Act of 2019, the IACC was required to (1) develop and annually update a strategic plan 
for autism research, (2) develop and annually update a summary of advances in autism research, and (3) 
monitor federal activities related to autism.  
Through these and other activities, the IACC provides guidance to HHS and partners with other federal 
departments, research and advocacy organizations, and the broader autism community to accelerate research 
and enhance services with the goal of positively impacting the lives of people on the autism spectrum and their 
families.  
For more information about the IACC, see https://iacc.hhs.gov/. 
 
Note: The IACC is a federal advisory committee established under the Autism CARES Act and chartered under 
the Federal Advisory Committee Act. The views expressed by the IACC do not represent the views of the U.S. 
Department of Health and Human Services or other Federal agencies and Departments. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
Editorial Note on References to Autism: The IACC supports the use of accessible language around autism in 
its publications. The terms "person with autism," "person with autism spectrum disorder (ASD)," "autistic 
person," and "person on the autism spectrum" are used interchangeably throughout this document. Some 
members of the autism community prefer one term, while others prefer another. The Committee respects the 
different opinions within the community on the use of this language and does not intend to endorse any 
particular preference. In addition, the term "autism" is generally used in this document, and “ASD” is used 
when referring speciﬁcally to the DSM-5-TR deﬁned diagnosis.

Introduction and Analysis Framework 
The Office of National Autism Coordination (ONAC) at the National Institute of Mental Health (NIMH), National 
Institutes of Health (NIH) supports the activities of the IACC. The ﬁrst IACC Autism Research Portfolio 
Analysis Report was issued in 2008 to provide the Committee with comprehensive information about the 
status of autism research funding among federal agencies and private research organizations in the United 
States. The 2008 Portfolio Analysis Report, along with extensive input from federal and public stakeholders, 
informed the development of the ﬁrst IACC Strategic Plan for Autism Spectrum Disorder Research that was 
published in 2009. 
The IACC Strategic Plan, now in its 9th edition, provides a framework to guide the efforts of federal and private 
funders of autism research. The IACC Portfolio Analysis Reports align autism research projects with 
Recommendations described in the IACC Strategic Plan. The reports gather data on funding for research 
projects related to Strategic Plan Recommendations and track funding trends over time. The IACC has used 
this information in their efforts to monitor autism research and determine progress made each year toward 
accomplishing the Recommendations in the IACC Strategic Plan.  
The 2021-2023 IACC Strategic Plan for Autism Research, Services, and Policy organizes research priorities 
around seven general topic areas represented as community-focused “Questions” (e.g., Question 1, "How can 
we improve identiﬁcation of autism?," which covers the topic of screening and diagnosis). The Committee 
developed an Aspirational Goal, or long-term vision, for each Question. Each Question is divided further into 
three research Recommendations (previously called Objectives) that address key research needs, gaps, and 
opportunities identiﬁed by the Committee. In addition, there are two cross-cutting Recommendations, one that 
includes research on sex differences in autism and one focusing on addressing gaps in health and well-being 
outcomes through autism research and services. This 2021-2022 IACC Autism Research Portfolio Analysis 
Report presents trends in autism research funding from 2008 to 2022 and alignment of research projects with 
the Recommendations of the 2021-2023 IACC Strategic Plan. The Strategic Plan also contains a Budget 
Recommendation as required by the Autism CARES Act. This report evaluates 2021 and 2022 U.S. autism 
funding against this benchmark of $685 million in autism research funding by 2025.

The IACC Strategic Plan Questions and Corresponding Research Areas 
ONAC requested information on 2021 and 2022 autism research projects funded by federal agencies and 
private organizations, including the annual funding amount and the relevance of each project to the seven 
critical Questions of the 2021-2023 IACC Strategic Plan. The seven IACC Strategic Plan Questions are also 
represented by corresponding research areas called Subcategories, illustrated in Figure 1. Subcategory 
classification divides the portfolio into topical areas relevant to research, such as “Brain Function and 
Circuits,” “Family Well-Being and Safety,” and “Data Tools.” This breakdown helps to illustrate the different 
types of research encompassed by the projects in the research portfolio. For the Subcategory analysis, each 
project was assigned to a Question and then a Subcategory based on the research area it addresses.

Autism Research Funders and Funding in 2021 and 2022 
Who funded autism research in 2021 and 2022? 
Fifteen federal departments and agencies and 18 private organizations contributed their research funding 
information for the 2021-2022 Autism Research Portfolio Analysis Report. These 33 funders are listed in Table 
1.1 The IACC and ONAC routinely review the funding landscape and offer opportunities for additional funders to 
join the portfolio analysis effort. This regular review enables the report to provide a comprehensive depiction of 
federal and private contributions to autism research in the United States. Additionally, new funders entering the 
field often expand the scope of autism research and fill in gaps in the field. For the present report, two federal 
funders (the Department of Labor and the HHS Office of the Assistant Secretary for Planning and 
Evaluation) and two private organizations (Easterseals Southern California and the FAR Fund) were identified 
and added to the analysis. Added funders accounted for 0.7% ($2.9 million) of total funding in 2021 and 0.3% 
($1.6 million) in 2022. The research projects that are added by these funders are important in understanding the 
autism research landscape but did not alter the overall funding trajectory observed in the portfolio. Some 
agencies and organizations included in previous years’ analyses did not have projects to report in 2021 or 2022 
or chose not to participate in the present analysis. Brief summaries of the mission areas of each agency and 
organization that contributed to the 2021-2022 Portfolio Analysis Report can be found in Appendix A. 
While ONAC has attempted to be as comprehensive as possible, other private funders not included in the 
portfolio analysis may also be funding research relevant to autism. For example, The Marcus Foundation has 
invested millions in the Marcus Autism Center, funding research on autism diagnosis and interventions. In 
addition, the Nancy Lurie Marks Family Foundation funds basic and translational autism research, as well as 
career development awards to support the next generation of autism researchers. Other funders such as the 
Sergey Brin Family Foundation and Wellcome Leap are also funding autism-relevant research. These examples 
illustrate that the broader private funding landscape for autism research likely extends beyond what is captured 
in this analysis.

How much autism research was funded in 2021 and 2022? 
Combined, the federal and private investment in autism research was $437.0 million in 2021 and spanned 
1,720 projects. Overall funding for autism research increased by 4.3% ($18.1 million) from 2020 to 2021. 
Funders newly added to the portfolio analysis accounted for 16.1% ($2.9 million) of the increase from 2020 to 
2021. Not including the contributions of these funders, funding increased by 3.6% ($15.2 million) from 2020 to 
2021. In 2022, U.S. autism research funding totaled $456.1 million with 1,899 projects, reflecting a 4.2% ($19.0 
million) increase in funding from 2021 to 2022. Funders newly added to the portfolio analysis accounted for 
8.4% ($1.6 million) of this increase. Without the contributions of these funders, funding increased by 4.0% 
($17.4 million) from 2021 to 2022.  
The relative proportions contributed by federal and private funders in 2021 and 2022 remained similar to 
previous years. In 2021, the federal government provided $364.9 million (919 projects) in autism research 
funding and accounted for 83.5% of overall funding, while private organizations provided $72.2 million (801 
projects) in funding, which accounted for 16.5% of the total funding (Figure 2). Federal agencies provided 
$357.4 million (951 projects) in autism research funding in 2022, accounting for 78.4% of total funding, and 
private organizations provided $98.6 million (948 projects), accounting for 21.6% of total funding (Figure 3). The 
increase in 2022 private funding was largely driven by the Simons Foundation Autism Research Initiative, which 
continued to support its SPARK (Simons Foundation Powering Autism Research) program and launched 
several new targeted funding initiatives with projects that began in 2022.

How many new research projects were added in 2021 and 2022 compared to ongoing research? 
To evaluate trends in funding directed towards the continuation of ongoing research versus newly initiated 
projects, the status of each project included in the portfolio analysis is classified as either “Ongoing” or “New.” 
Ongoing projects were active in a previous year, and new projects became active and received funding for the 
first time in the specified year of analysis. Since most research projects are funded over multiple years, a larger 
number of ongoing projects compared to new projects is expected. In 2021, 75.0% ($327.7 million) of overall 
autism research funding went to ongoing projects, while 25.0% ($109.3 million) went to new projects. In 2022, 
67.2% ($306.6 million) of funding was assigned to ongoing projects, and 32.8% ($149.5 million) was assigned to 
new projects. This breakdown is similar to historical trends, which show that ongoing projects typically account 
for 70-80% of total funding and new projects account for 20-30% (Figure 4).

What funding trends were observed?  
• 
Overall, autism research funding increased in 2021 and 2022 (Figure 5). 
o In 2020, the combined federal and private investment in autism research was $418.9 million. 
o In 2021, the combined federal and private investment in autism research was $437.0 million, an 
increase of 4.3% from 2020. 
o In 2022, the combined federal and private investment in autism research was $456.1 million, an 
increase of 4.4% from 2021.  
• 
The amount of federal investment in autism research increased by 5.5% ($19.0 million) in 2021 ($364.9 
million) from 2020 ($345.8 million). In 2022, the federal investment in autism research decreased by 
2.0% ($7.5 million).   
• 
The amount of private investment in autism research decreased by 1.3% ($0.9 million) in 2021 ($72.2 
million) from 2020 ($73.1 million). In 2022, private investment in autism research increased by 36.7% 
($26.5 million). 
• 
As described in previous IACC Portfolio Analysis Reports, the American Recovery and Reinvestment Act 
(ARRA) provided an additional $63.9 million in 2009 and $59.9 million in 2010 to support autism 
research projects. This created a temporary increase in total autism research funding during those 
years, resulting in a high of $408.6 million in 2010. In the years following, funding levels decreased in 
comparison to 2010. With steady increases in recent years, autism funding levels have since surpassed 
the previous high in 2010. 
• 
According to an analysis of the impact of inﬂation over time, however, autism research funding peaked 
in terms of purchasing power in 2010 at $385.2 million in inﬂation-adjusted 2008 constant dollars 
(Figure 6).

In 2008, autism research funding totaled $222.2 million. From 2008 to 2022, funding increased by 105.2% 
($233.8 million), demonstrating an overall trajectory of growth. However, funding has varied from one year to 
the next during that time (Figure 5). An infusion of funds from the ARRA in 2009 and 2010 took autism research 
funding to a high of $408.6 million in 2010, but funding then decreased in 2011. There was an increase in 2012, 
followed by decreases in 2013 and 2014. Steady growth occurred from 2015 through 2019. In 2020, funding 
levels decreased by 1.2% ($5.3 million) compared to 2019. This was followed by increases in autism research 
funding in 2021 and 2022, and the autism research portfolio was funded at its highest level ever at $456.1 
million in 2022. 
 
 
 
18 
 
Contributors to Funding Trends 
Over the years of portfolio analysis tracking, ﬂuctuations in funding have been observed, which can result from 
factors such as the release of new initiatives and sunsetting of other initiatives, changes in organization 
budgets and priorities, changes in government appropriations, and the effects of using certain funding 
mechanisms. For example, some funders allocate all funding to a project in the ﬁrst year, while others disburse 
the funds over regularly spaced intervals. These different disbursement mechanisms may result in ﬂuctuation 
of overall funding levels from one year to another. Additionally, some funders may not have an established and 
consistent autism research portfolio and thus may provide one-time or sporadic funding for speciﬁc autism-
related projects or initiatives. Availability of resources for different funders, particularly those in the private 
sector, may also vary from year to year.  
In the previous Portfolio Analysis Report, a decrease in funding was observed from 2019 to 2020. The above 
factors may have contributed. In addition, 2020 funding levels may have been impacted by the coronavirus 
disease 2019 (COVID-19) pandemic, which affected research funding across many scientiﬁc disciplines. 
Analysis in the present Portfolio Analysis Report indicates that autism research funding in 2021 and 2022 
regained a positive trajectory of growth.

Where is autism research being funded in the United States? 
Figures 7 and 8 show the distribution of autism research projects across the United States funded by both 
federal agencies and private organizations in 2021 and 2022, respectively. The maps show that research is 
concentrated along the east and west coasts and in major metropolitan areas or areas with large universities in 
the middle portion of the country. 
 
Figure 7. A map of the United States displaying the geographic distribution and number of autism research 
projects funded by federal agencies and private organizations in 2021. 
20

projects funded by federal agencies and private organizations in 2022. 
 
The U.S. institutions that received the largest amounts of funding in 2021 are the University of California, Los 
Angeles (UCLA), Yale University, and the University of California, Davis (UC Davis). In 2022, the institutions that 
received the largest amounts of funding are Yale University, UC Davis, and UC San Francisco (UCSF). UCLA has 
many investigators collaborating on major autism research initiatives, such as the Baby Siblings Consortium, 
the Autism Sequencing Consortium (ASC), and Simons Simplex Collection (SSC). Both the ASC and the SSC 
are major initiatives investigating the genetics of autism. Yale University is similar in that researchers at the 
institution are collaborating on several large multisite research projects, such as the Autism Biomarkers 
Consortium for Clinical Trials (ABC-CT) and the SSC. UC Davis includes researchers involved in the Baby 
Siblings Consortium and SPARK for Autism, which also focuses on the genetic basis of autism, and UCSF has 
researchers participating in large research projects as part of NIH Cooperative Agreements. Many of the other 
institutions with large amounts of funding are involved in large genetic, biological, and environmental research 
networks. Tables 2 and 3 provide additional information about the institutions and states that received the 
largest amounts of autism research funding in 2021, and Tables 4 and 5 provide information on institutions and 
states that received the largest amount of autism research funding in 2022.

Analysis of Potential Duplication 
The Autism CARES Act of 2014 (Public Law 113-157) required the HHS Secretary to designate a National 
Autism Coordinator (NAC) to “implement autism spectrum disorder activities, taking into account the strategic 
plan developed by the Interagency Autism Coordinating Committee and ensure that autism spectrum disorder 
activities of the Department of Health and Human Services and of other Federal departments and agencies are 
not unnecessarily duplicative.” To support the NAC in carrying out these duties, ONAC analyzed the 2021 and 
2022 autism research portfolio for potential duplication based on information included in the project title, 
abstract or description, principal investigator (PI), institution, and project start and end dates. The results of 
this analysis are included in the Portfolio Analysis Report to assist the IACC in making “recommendations [in 
the Strategic Plan] to ensure that autism spectrum disorder research, and services and support activities to the 
extent practicable, of the Department of Health and Human Services and of other Federal departments and 
agencies are not unnecessarily duplicative,” as required by the Autism CARES Act.  
For the purpose of this analysis, potential duplication is defined as either: 
1. The same PI is receiving funding from two or more funders to conduct the same project at the same 
time that aims to answer the same research questions, using the same methods and model systems, in 
the same study population, without the explicit aim of replicating previously reported results.  
2. Multiple PIs are receiving funding from one or more funders to conduct the same project at the same 
time that aims to answer the same research questions, using the same methods and model systems, in 
the same study population, without the explicit aim of replicating previously reported results.  
In some instances, funders may co-fund projects, either for the same PI or multiple PIs working collaboratively 
on one project. PIs may also seek subsequent funding to continue work on an existing project, either from the 
same funder or from a different funder. In addition, some supplemental projects may also include the same 
abstract or description as the parent project. These instances are not considered potential duplication.  
After reviewing all projects, ONAC did not identify any potential duplication in the 2021 or 2022 autism research 
portfolio.

Question 1: Screening and Diagnosis 
ASPIRATIONAL GOAL: Provide a timely diagnosis for people on the autism spectrum, so they can be 
linked to appropriate interventions, services, and supports to maximize positive outcomes. 
RESEARCH FOCUS OF QUESTION 1 
Question 1 of the IACC Strategic Plan (How can we improve identification of autism?) pertains to the issues 
surrounding screening for and diagnosis of autism, with a focus on early identification so that children will have 
the opportunity to receive interventions and supports that can lead to improved outcomes. The 
Recommendations within this Question of the Strategic Plan include research to develop and improve 
biomarkers, screening tools, and diagnostic instruments to aid in early identification of autism. Question 1 
topics also include research to improve access to diagnostic services and strengthen the evidence base for the 
benefits of early detection of autism. In addition, the Committee prioritized the need for screening and 
diagnostic tools for use in adolescents and adults. Projects addressing issues related to adult screening and 
diagnosis are captured within Question 6 of the Strategic Plan (focused on issues relevant to transition-age 
youth and adults on the autism spectrum). 
ANALYSIS OF 2021-2022 QUESTION 1 PORTFOLIO 
When analyzing the distribution of research dollars across the seven Question areas of the IACC Strategic Plan, 
projects assigned to Question 1 comprised 6.8% of total autism research funding in 2021 and 2022 ($29.6 
million and $30.9 million, respectively). A total of 103 projects were assigned to Question 1 in 2021, which was 
6.0% of all projects. In 2022, Question 1 had 108 projects or 5.7% of all projects. The largest funder of research 
in this area for both years was the National Institutes of Health, followed by the Simons Foundation in 2021 and 
the Department of Defense – Army in 2022. Figures 30 and 31 provide an overview of each of the three 
Recommendations within Question 1 as well as the number of projects assigned to each Recommendation. 
In 2021 and 2022, all three Question 1 Recommendations were in progress and received funding. The 
Recommendation that received the bulk of Question 1 funding was Recommendation 1.3, which aims to 
develop and adapt screening and diagnostic tools for detecting autism (2021: 81.7%, $24.2 million, 82 projects; 
2022: 71.9%, $22.2 million, 88 projects). In 2021, this was followed by Recommendation 1.1, which was 14.5% 
of Question 1 funding and focuses on supporting research on how early detection of autism influences 
outcomes ($4.3 million, 8 projects). This Recommendation received 9.2% of 2022 funding ($2.9 million, 4 
projects). Recommendation 1.2 on improving access to early detection and services received 1.2% ($354,875) 
of Question 1 funding in 2021 and had 10 projects. In 2022, Recommendation 1.2 received 16.7% of Question 
funding ($5.1 million, 13 projects).  Three projects were categorized as Core/Other in 2021 and 2022 (i.e., 
projects not specific to Question 1 Recommendations) (2021: 2.6%, $775,749; 2022: 2.1%, $662,748). These 
included a project investigating the etiologies of “complex” versus “essential” autism, a project that examines 
preverbal social learning in children with autism with communication challenges, and a project investigating 
the impact of the medical home model on early identification and intervention receipt.

QUESTION 1 SUBCATEGORY ANALYSIS 
All 2021 and 2022 autism projects were categorized into “Subcategories,” which are broad research topics or 
themes. Even if a project did not fit within a particular Recommendation of the Strategic Plan, it was still 
assigned to a specific Subcategory. This enables a comprehensive understanding of the distribution of all 
projects across the research topics aligned with each Question area. Overall, projects in Question 1 were 
divided into four Subcategories: Diagnostic and Screening Tools; Early Signs and Biomarkers; 
Phenotypes/Subgroups; and Spectrum of Characteristics (Figures 32 and 33). 
Of the four Subcategories, the largest proportion of 2021 and 2022 funding was devoted to Diagnostic and 
Screening Tools for autism (2021: 55.0%, $16.3 million, 59 projects; 2022: 69.1%, $21.3 million, 68 projects). 
Identifying Early Signs and Biomarkers was the second largest research investment in Question 1 (2021: 
25.0%, $7.4 million, 27 projects; 2022: 13.4%, $4.2 million, 27 projects). Included in this Subcategory were 
biological indicators (including genetic, metabolic, and brain structure/connectivity) and behavioral biomarkers 
that can be used for screening/diagnosis or to measure response to interventions. Projects assigned to 
Spectrum of Characteristics received the next largest proportion of funding for Question 1 (2021: 11.4%, $3.4 
million, 11 projects; 2022: 9.0%, $2.8 million, 8 projects). This Subcategory captures projects that seek to 
define the broad range of autism characteristics, including variations in neurocognitive development and 
differences in social communication, language, cognitive ability, sensory sensitivities, and executive

functioning ability. Lastly, identifying Phenotypes/Subgroups of people with autism received 8.5% of Question 
1 funding (2021: $2.5 million, 6 projects; 2022: $2.6 million, 5 projects).

Question 2: Biology 
ASPIRATIONAL GOAL: Discover the roles of brain development, cognition, and physiological function in 
autism and its co-occurring conditions to enable the development of effective, targeted interventions and 
societal accommodations that promote positive outcomes across the lifespan. 
RESEARCH FOCUS OF QUESTION 2 
Question 2 (What is the biology underlying autism?) seeks to understand the biological differences and 
mechanisms in early development and throughout life that contribute to autism features, as well as 
characterization of the behavioral and cognitive aspects of autism. The aim of the research represented by 
Question 2 is to understand the biological processes underlying autism from the molecular level to sensory, 
motor, behavioral, cognitive, and physiological development and functioning. Projects range from basic 
neuroscience using cellular and animal models to clinical studies. In addition, Question 2 addresses physical 
and mental health conditions that co-occur with autism. 
ANALYSIS OF 2021-2022 QUESTION 2 PORTFOLIO 
Among the seven Question areas of the IACC Strategic Plan, Question 2 accounted for the largest portion of the 
autism research portfolio in both 2021 and 2022, growing by over $150 million since 2008. Research on the 
Biology of autism (Question 2) comprised 43.7% of total funding and 36.3% of all projects in 2021 ($191.0 
million, 625 projects). In 2022, Question 2 funding made up 41.9% ($191.2 million) of total funding and 35.4% 
(673 projects) of all projects. Among federal agencies and private organizations, the National Institutes of 
Health, the Simons Foundation, and the Department of Defense - Army provided the largest investments for 
Question 2 funding. Figures 35 and 36 provide an overview of funding for the three Question 2 
Recommendations as well as the number of projects belonging to each Recommendation. 
All three Recommendations in Question 2 were in progress and received funding in 2021 and 2022. 
Recommendation 2.1 had the most projects, with 84.0% of Question 2 funding in 2021 ($160.4 million, 532 
projects) and 83.8% of funding in 2022 ($160.3 million, 569 projects). The aim of this Recommendation is to 
better understand the neurodevelopmental, molecular, and brain processes that contribute to autism. The next 
largest portion of funding went to Recommendation 2.2, which emphasizes research on understanding co-
occurring physical and mental health conditions (2021: 8.4%, $16.1 million, 60 projects; 2022: 9.1%, $17.5 
million, 71 projects). Recommendation 2.3, which focuses on supporting large-scale longitudinal studies of 
autism that assess the natural lifespan, received $13.6 million in funding (7.1% of the Question 2 portfolio) and 
spanned 27 projects in 2021, with $12.1 million in funding (6.3% of Question 2 funding) and 28 projects in 2022. 
Less than 1% of Question 2 funding was assigned to Core/Other (2021: $909,694, 6 projects; 2022: $1.4 million, 
5 projects). Projects assigned to Core/Other included research studying eye morphology in individuals with 
autism, efforts to test new technologies to understand the biology of autism, as well as support for statistical 
analyses of large data sets.

The Subcategory analysis is particularly useful for Question 2 in understanding the distribution of research on

and thus Question 2 was divided into several Subcategories. These include Biosignatures; Brain Function and 
Circuits; Cognition, Communication, and Behavior; Co-Occurring Conditions; Immune/Metabolic Pathways; 
Molecular Pathways; Neuropathology; and Sensory and Motor Function (Figures 37 and 38). 
As in previous years, the Question 2 Subcategory with the largest portion of funding in 2021 was Molecular 
Pathways (2021: 39.3%, $75.1 million, 234 projects; 2022: 35.5%, $67.9 million, 234 projects), which includes 
projects seeking to understand how specific genes, proteins, and other molecules interact to influence autism. 
Research exploring Biosignatures, such as patterns of gene expression, hormone levels, or structural

Summary and Conclusion 
The 2021-2022 IACC Autism Research Portfolio Analysis Report represents the 14th and 15th year of data 
collected and the tenth comprehensive report of U.S. autism research funding across both federal and private 
sectors. In 2021, funding for autism research among both federal and private funders totaled $437.0 million 
and spanned 1,720 projects. In 2022, U.S. autism research funding totaled $456.1 million for 1,899 projects. 
From 2008-2022, autism research has shown an overall upward trend in funding, increasing by 105.2% since 
2008.  
For this current edition of the Portfolio Analysis Report, project information was collected from 33 federal and 
private funders; the varied missions of the different funders are reflected in the autism research portfolio 
across the seven Questions of the Strategic Plan. Four additional autism research funders were added to the 
portfolio analysis, providing an updated and more comprehensive view of the autism research funding 
landscape. While added funders did not have a large impact on overall funding trends, emerging new funders 
fill in gaps and increase the scope and breadth of autism research. Comparable to previous years, federal 
agencies funded approximately 80% of autism research while private organizations contributed approximately 
20% of funding. Among the participating funders, the National Institutes of Health continued to contribute the 
largest federal (and overall) investment in autism research, and the Simons Foundation was the largest private 
funder. 
One of the key aims of the Portfolio Analysis Report is to analyze and present information regarding funding that 
addresses the research priorities outlined in the IACC Strategic Plan. This report represents the first analysis to 
measure research funding against the Recommendations of the 2021-2023 IACC Strategic Plan. Every 
Recommendation in the 2021-2023 IACC Strategic Plan had associated projects and funding in 2021 and 2022, 
indicating that the priority areas identified by the Committee were also identified and supported as priority 
areas by federal and private research funders.  
Biology (Question 2) continued to be the largest research area funded in 2021 and 2022. In addition, as in 2019 
and 2020, Genetic and Environmental Factors (Question 3) had the next largest amount of funding. Services 
and Supports (Question 5) received the next largest amount of funding in 2021, increasing by $11.2 million from 
2020 to 2021. This was followed by Infrastructure and Prevalence (Question 7), Interventions (Question 4), and 
Screening and Diagnosis (Question 1). Research on Lifespan (Question 6) continued to receive the smallest 
amount of 2021 funding in comparison to other areas. In 2022, Interventions (Question 4) was the third most 
well-funded Question area, followed by Infrastructure and Prevalence (Question 7). For the first time, Lifespan 
(Question 6) did not have the smallest amount of funding in 2022 and surpassed funding for Services and 
Supports (Question 5) and Screening and Diagnosis (Question 1). The two Cross-Cutting Recommendations 
also showed significant growth in 2021. Research focused on sex differences increased by $24.4 million, and 
research focused on gaps in health and well-being outcomes increased by $16.3 million. Both Cross-Cutting 
Recommendations also saw increases in funding, albeit a smaller amount, in 2022. New investments from 
federal and private funders in these areas reflect responsiveness to the evolving needs of the autism 
community and alignment with the Recommendations of the IACC Strategic Plan. 
As described in the Budget Recommendation section of the 2021-2023 IACC Strategic Plan for Autism, an 
infusion of resources in areas such as lifespan, interventions, and services may help to broaden the scope of 
autism research to more effectively serve autistic people of all ages, all levels of ability, and in communities 
across the nation. With expanded resources and a workforce that includes those with lived experience, the full 
104 
 
range of autism research will have the potential to make significant advancements in the coming years and 
greatly impact the lives of individuals across the autism spectrum and lifespan.

affected. Serving as a leader in the rare disease community, TSCA’s goals are to accelerate research, improve 
access and quality of care, support and empower constituents, educate and mobilize to increase investment, 
and build and strengthen organization. An estimated 40-50% of individuals with TSC have autism, and TSC is a 
leading genetic cause of syndromic autism. TSCA funds research that focuses on the connection between 
autism and TSC.

Appendix B: Subcategory Definitions 
 
Question 1: SCREENING AND DIAGNOSIS  
Diagnostic and Screening Tools  
This Subcategory includes projects that are developing new autism diagnostic and screening tests, as well as 
those establishing the usefulness of new or revised assessments for autism features. It also encompasses 
projects aimed at improving early identification services and adapting clinical assessments for use in different 
community settings and countries in addition to the United States.  
Early Signs and Biomarkers  
Projects which use a variety of methods to search for signs of autism in very young children (generally under age 
3) that could be used for diagnosis, such as eye-tracking, physiological measures, and autism-specific 
behavioral patterns are included in this Subcategory. More examples include projects investigating metabolic 
measures, such as the levels of specific chemicals, hormones, or proteins in the blood that could be used as 
biomarkers of autism.  
Phenotypes/Subgroups  
Included in this Subcategory are projects aimed at identifying distinct subgroups of people with autism, or 
those that share common morphological, physiological, or behavioral features. Projects in this Subcategory 
use a variety of methods to identify and distinguish these groups.  
Spectrum of Characteristics  
These projects seek to define the broad range of autism characteristics, including both biological and 
behavioral features. Among these studies are those that examine how children and adults with autism vary in 
their development of social communication, language, cognitive ability, sensory sensitivities, and executive 
functioning ability. Other projects seek to understand how differences in neurocognitive development can 
contribute to phenotypic variability in those with an autism diagnosis.  
 
Question 2: BIOLOGY 
Biosignatures  
Because there is so much heterogeneity among individuals with autism, research to understand how certain 
subgroups of individuals that share certain behavioral or biological characteristics could help clarify some of 
the underlying biology in autism. This can be done by searching for certain biological factors (“signatures”), 
such as patterns of gene expression, hormone levels, or structural differences in the brain, that define a 
particular subgroup. Many of these projects try to make the connection between certain genes with a known or 
suspected link to autism and an observable characteristic, or phenotype, that they cause. 
Brain Function and Circuits 
114 
 
Studies in this Subcategory explore the structure and activity of the brain and underlying neural systems 
involved in autism, including functional connections between brain regions. Many projects seek to identify the 
neural networks and circuits underlying communication and language processing, social interactions, and 
behaviors. These studies frequently employ imaging techniques, such as functional magnetic resonance 
imaging (fMRI) and diffusion tensor imaging (DTI), and other physiological measures of brain activity, such as 
electroencephalography (EEG).  
Cognition, Communication, and Behavior   
These are studies of psychological and mental processes, including memory, producing and understanding 
language, solving problems, and making decisions. Projects in this Subcategory also include those that 
investigate theory of mind, social cognition, communication, emotion regulation, and recall and memory.  
Co-Occurring Conditions  
Research on co-occurring physical and mental health conditions and their overlap with autism is included here, 
such as seizures/epilepsy, sleep disorders, gastrointestinal issues, autoimmune disorders, attention 
deﬁcit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD), anxiety, and depression. Included are projects that investigate the 
unique presentation of these conditions in autism, as well as potential common underlying mechanisms. 
Immune/Metabolic Pathways  
These projects focus on understanding the biological mechanisms of metabolism and the immune system that 
may be altered in autism, typically using cell cultures and animal models. This largely includes studies on 
inflammation and inflammatory molecules (i.e., cytokines), as well as on the role of mitochondria, energy 
metabolism, and oxidative stress. Also included in this group are projects seeking to identify specific immune 
and metabolic triggers in early prenatal and post-natal life, such as maternal infection, maternal 
autoantibodies, and environmental exposures.  
Molecular Pathways  
This Subcategory includes studies on specific molecules and proteins (other than the immune and metabolic 
systems) that may be involved in the development of autism and related genetic disorders (e.g., Fragile X 
syndrome and Rett syndrome). Many of these projects use animal and cellular models to explore the biological 
effects of specific candidate genes and to identify common molecular pathways, including alterations in 
synaptic functioning and intracellular signaling cascades.  
Neuropathology  
These projects typically include post-mortem examination of brain tissue from individuals with autism. Many of 
the studies in this Subcategory explore how the architecture of the brain may be altered in individuals with 
autism or how gene expression varies in different areas of the autistic brain.  
Sensory and Motor Function  
Projects in this Subcategory explore the neural underpinnings of sensory differences and motor skills in autistic 
children and adults and assess visual, auditory, and other sensory processes in the brain.  
115 
 
 
Question 3: GENETIC AND ENVIRONMENTAL FACTORS 
Environmental Factors  
This Subcategory includes projects investigating environmental factors that may contribute to the development 
of autism. Examples include studies of how changes of the microbiome, environmental exposures, assistive 
reproductive treatments, paternal factors, and maternal factors (such as diet, medications taken during 
pregnancy or to induce labor, perinatal conditions, child and maternal response to immune challenges) may 
contribute to autism. Also included in this Subcategory are registries where many of these factors can be 
tracked simultaneously.  
Epigenetics  
Epigenetics is the study of how changes in behaviors, physiology, and/or the environment (including paternal 
and maternal factors) can affect gene activity. Unlike genetic changes, which change the actual sequence of 
nucleotides in DNA, epigenetic changes can modify how DNA sequences are read and how genes are 
expressed (such as through methylation of DNA) without changes in the DNA sequence itself. These changes 
can be transient and reversible, or they may be heritable in some circumstances. Projects in this Subcategory 
seek to identify some of the influences that may lead to these epigenetic changes and how these epigenetic 
changes may contribute to autism development.  
Gene-Environment  
These studies include efforts to identify and understand how the interactions of environmental factors 
(including paternal and maternal factors), genetic susceptibility, and/or human physiology (e.g., the immune 
system, metabolic processes) may contribute to the development of autism. (Note: While epigenetic studies 
are a subset of gene-environment studies, they are tracked as a separate Subcategory because there is a 
substantial number of these projects.) 
Genetic Factors  
Projects in this Subcategory seek to identify new genes that are implicated in increased probability of autism or 
to better understand genetic factors that were previously identified. 
 
Question 4: INTERVENTIONS 
Behavioral  
Projects in this Subcategory involve a wide array of behavioral research and training methods, including applied 
behavior analysis (ABA), naturalistic developmental behavioral interventions (NDBI), cognitive-behavioral 
therapy (CBT), discrete trial training, Early Start Denver Model, imitation training, joint attention training, Lovaas 
method, pivotal response training, sibling-mediated interventions, and social skills training.  
Complementary, Dietary, and Alternative  
116 
 
This Subcategory includes research on acupressure; acupuncture; antioxidants; use of dietary and nutritional 
supplements, vitamins, and minerals; probiotics; and special diets (e.g., gluten-free, casein-free).  
Educational  
Nearly all research in classroom settings falls under this Subcategory, including curricula, educational best 
practices, education programs, math and reading training, positive behavioral supports, special education 
programs, TEACCH (Treatment and Education of Autistic and Related Communication-Handicapped Children), 
and the “Social Stories” approach.  
Medical/Pharmacologic  
This Subcategory includes research on drugs (e.g., antidepressants, anticonvulsants, antipsychotics, 
anxiolytics, melatonin, and stimulants) to treat autism and its co-occurring conditions, as well as medical 
therapies such as transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS).  
Model Systems/Therapeutic Targets  
Animal models of autism and those that are being used to develop or test new drug treatments, as well as cell 
lines used to discover new drug targets or to screen potential drug candidates, are included in this 
Subcategory.  
Occupational, Physical, and Sensory-Based  
Therapies in this Subcategory encompass art therapy, motor training (including fine motor skills such as 
handwriting as well as gross motor training involving balance and posture), music therapy, occupational 
therapy, animal therapy, physical activity plans and exercise therapy (bike riding, swimming), physical therapy, 
sensory integration, programs to increase familiarity with medical procedures, and training in self-care and 
daily living skills. Note: Projects focused specifically on the adolescent/adult population and self-care and daily 
living skills are found in Question 6, “Daily Living Skills.” 
Technology-Based  
Augmentative and alternative communication (AAC), computer applications and software, picture exchange 
communication system (PECS), social robots, interventions designed for delivery via telehealth and online 
platforms, video modeling and virtual reality (including virtual and 3D environments to mimic social situations), 
and wearable sensors are all examples of the types of technology in this Subcategory’s projects. 
 
Question 5: SERVICES AND SUPPORTS 
Accessibility of Community Programs  
These projects provide support in creating autistic- and sensory-friendly programs and environments at events 
and community spaces, or increasing accessibility of existing programs and resources, such as at libraries and 
museums. Also included are projects that focus on social, communication, and leisure skills to enhance 
autistic individuals’ participation in sports, recreation, and social activities in fully integrated settings and to 
build successful relationships. 
117 
 
Family Well-Being and Safety  
Studies in this Subcategory evaluate issues of caregiver stress, sibling mental health, and measures of well-
being for individuals with autism and their families, as well as assess programs to help parents and caregivers 
navigate the service system. It also surveys safety issues for those on the autism spectrum, including 
wandering, law enforcement interactions, and bullying. 
Implementation Science and Service Delivery  
This Subcategory includes efforts to implement and scale up evidence-based interventions in real-world 
settings, aiming to ensure fidelity and improve efficacy and cost-effectiveness of services. It includes programs 
involving web-based curricula and interventions as well as telehealth methodology, all of which could benefit 
those in underserved areas. Various parent training projects (to deliver a behavioral therapy, for example) using 
web-based methods such as teleconsultation and video feedback make distributing the training programs 
cost-effective and accessible across the country.  
Practitioner Training  
Projects in this Subcategory seek to increase skill levels in service providers, including medical and emergency 
service providers, law enforcement and justice officials, direct support workers, parents and legal guardians, 
education staff, and public service workers.  
Services Utilization and Access  
These projects include surveys of service systems available in different states, evaluations of patterns of 
service use among children with autism, comprehensive resources for autism services, and efforts to 
coordinate and increase accessibility of services for people with autism. They also evaluate obstacles to 
services access. 
 
Question 6: LIFESPAN 
Community Integration Supports and Services  
This Subcategory includes projects that enhance community services, programs, and environments to increase 
integration of autistic youth and adults. Also included are development of interventions and supports to 
increase community involvement among transition-age youth and adults on the autism spectrum.  
Daily Living Skills 
Research in this Subcategory focuses on independent living skills training (e.g., self-care, executive function, 
self-determination, self-advocacy, goal setting) for youth and adults with autism. Also included in this 
Subcategory are transportation use/driver education programs, as well as programs focused on sexual health. 
Health Outcomes  
Projects in this Subcategory focus on understanding and improving physical, mental, and behavioral health-
related outcomes for youth and adults, including interventions for autism and co-occurring conditions 
118 
 
experienced by adolescents/adults, such as substance use, depression and anxiety in adulthood, and 
dementia experienced in older adulthood. 
Health Care Systems/Health Care Transitions  
These projects are focused on efforts to improve patient-provider experiences and interactions across the 
lifespan; this category includes screening and diagnostic tools focused on youth and adults (not solely autism-
specific tools).  
Transition to Adulthood and Postsecondary Outcomes  
These projects focus on services, tools, and interventions that are helpful to youth making the transition out of 
high school. Often, these focus on transition planning, education, and employment. This Subcategory also 
focuses on young adulthood and projects that support postsecondary outcomes such as college experiences, 
employment, and quality of life outcomes. 
 
Question 7: INFRASTRUCTURE AND PREVALENCE 
Biobanks  
A biobank is a type of facility that stores human biological samples for use in research. Projects in this 
Subcategory support the collection of DNA and tissue samples from autistic individuals. 
Data Tools  
These projects include bioinformatics databases to store genetic, phenotypic, and other medical information 
from autism patients. They also support infrastructure for several of these major databases to interact and 
disseminate data to the community and stakeholders.  
Prevalence Studies  
Research that measures prevalence of autism is contained in this Subcategory, including the Autism and 
Developmental Disabilities Monitoring (ADDM) Network sites maintained by the CDC.  
Research Infrastructure  
This Subcategory includes coordinating centers that support multiple research projects by running tests, 
analyzing data, providing statistical analyses, and disseminating research to the community. These projects 
also support facilities that operate large, shared instruments used by several scientists to test research 
samples.  
Research Recruitment and Clinical Care  
Projects in this Subcategory help increase participation in research studies and conduct medical evaluations 
for the participants, often collecting data that can be used for multiple studies.  
Research Workforce Development  
119 
 
Workshops, conferences, and training programs that aim to expand the research workforce, enhance 
interdisciplinary research training, and recruit early-career scientists into the autism field are included in this 
Subcategory. Also included are efforts to recruit and support autistic researchers.
